1	# Brand register
2	
3	When design IS the product: brand sites, landing pages, marketing surfaces, campaign pages, portfolios, long-form content, about pages. The deliverable is the design itself; a visitor's impression is the thing being made.
4	
5	The register spans every genre. A tech brand (Stripe, Linear, Vercel). A luxury brand (a hotel, a fashion house). A consumer product (a restaurant, a travel site, a CPG packaging page). A creative studio, an agency portfolio, a band's album page. They all share the stance (*communicate, not transact*) and diverge wildly in aesthetic. Don't collapse them into a single look.
6	
7	## The brand slop test
8	
9	If someone could look at this and say "AI made that" without hesitation, it's failed. The bar is distinctiveness; a visitor should ask "how was this made?", not "which AI made this?"
10	
11	Brand isn't a neutral register. AI-generated landing pages have flooded the internet, and average is no longer findable. Restraint without intent now reads as mediocre, not refined. Brand surfaces need a POV, a specific audience, a willingness to risk strangeness. Go big or go home.
12	
13	**The second slop test: aesthetic lane.** Before committing to moves, name the reference. A Klim-style specimen page is one lane; Stripe-minimal is another; Liquid-Death-acid-maximalism is another. Don't drift into editorial-magazine aesthetics on a brief that isn't editorial. A hiking brand with Cormorant italic drop caps has the wrong register within the register.
14	
15	Then the inverse test: in one sentence, describe what you're about to build the way a competitor would describe theirs. If that sentence fits the modal landing page in the category, restart.
16	
17	## Typography
18	
19	### Font selection procedure
20	
21	Every project. Never skip.
22	
23	1. Read the brief. Write three concrete brand-voice words. Not "modern" or "elegant," but "warm and mechanical and opinionated" or "calm and clinical and careful." Physical-object words.
24	2. List the three fonts you'd reach for by reflex. If any appear in the reflex-reject list below, reject them; they are training-data defaults and they create monoculture.
25	3. Browse a real catalog (Google Fonts, Pangram Pangram, Future Fonts, Adobe Fonts, ABC Dinamo, Klim, Velvetyne) with the three words in mind. Find the font for the brand as a *physical object*: a museum caption, a 1970s terminal manual, a fabric label, a cheap-newsprint children's book, a concert poster, a receipt from a mid-century diner. Reject the first thing that "looks designy."
26	4. Cross-check. "Elegant" is not necessarily serif. "Technical" is not necessarily sans. "Warm" is not Fraunces. If the final pick lines up with the original reflex, start over.
27	
28	### Reflex-reject list
29	
30	Training-data defaults. Ban list. Look further:
31	
32	Fraunces · Newsreader · Lora · Crimson · Crimson Pro · Crimson Text · Playfair Display · Cormorant · Cormorant Garamond · Syne · IBM Plex Mono · IBM Plex Sans · IBM Plex Serif · Space Mono · Space Grotesk · Inter · DM Sans · DM Serif Display · DM Serif Text · Outfit · Plus Jakarta Sans · Instrument Sans · Instrument Serif
33	
34	### Reflex-reject aesthetic lanes
35	
36	Parallel to the font list. Currently saturated aesthetic families that have flooded brand surfaces. If a brief lands in one of these lanes without a register reason that *requires* it (a literal magazine, a literal terminal, a literal industrial signage system), it's the second-order training reflex: the trap one tier deeper than picking a Fraunces font. Look further.
37	
38	- **Editorial-typographic.** Display serif (often italic) + small mono labels + ruled separators + monochromatic restraint. Klim-influenced, magazine-cover affectation. By 2026, every Stripe-adjacent and Notion-adjacent brand has landed here. The fingerprint: three rule-separated columns, an italic Fraunces / Recoleta / Newsreader headline, lowercase track-spaced metadata, no imagery.
39	
40	(More entries land here on the same cadence the font list updates. Brutalist-utility and acid-maximalism may join when they saturate. Removing entries when they fall back below saturation is also fine.)
41	
42	The reflex-reject lists apply to **new design choices**. When the existing brand has already committed to a font or a lane as part of its identity, identity-preservation wins; variants on an existing surface don't second-guess what's already shipping. The reflex-reject lists are for greenfield decisions and for departure-mode variants in [live.md](live.md).
43	
44	### Pairing and voice
45	
46	Distinctive + refined is the goal. The specific shape depends on the brand:
47	
48	- **Editorial / long-form / luxury**: display serif + sans body (a magazine shape).
49	- **Tech / dev tools / fintech**: one committed sans, usually; custom-tight tracking, strong weight contrast inside a single family.
50	- **Consumer / food / travel**: warmer pairings, often a humanist sans plus a script or display serif.
51	- **Creative studios / agencies**: rule-breaking welcome. Mono-only, or display-only, or custom-drawn type as voice.
52	
53	Two families minimum is the rule *only* when the voice needs it. A single well-chosen family with committed weight/size contrast is stronger than a timid display+body pair.
54	
55	Vary across projects. If the last brief was a serif-display landing page, this one isn't.
56	
57	### Scale
58	
59	Modular scale, fluid `clamp()` for headings, ≥1.25 ratio between steps. Flat scales (1.1× apart) read as uncommitted.
60	
61	Light text on dark backgrounds: add 0.05–0.1 to line-height. Light type reads as lighter weight and needs more breathing room.
62	
63	## Color
64	
65	Brand surfaces have permission for Committed, Full palette, and Drenched strategies. Use them. A single saturated color spread across a hero is not excess; it's voice. A beige-and-muted-slate landing page ignores the register.
66	
67	- Name a real reference before picking a strategy. "Klim Type Foundry #ff4500 orange drench", "Stripe purple-on-white restraint", "Liquid Death acid-green full palette", "Mailchimp yellow full palette", "Condé Nast Traveler muted navy restraint", "Vercel pure black monochrome". Unnamed ambition becomes beige.
68	- Palette IS voice. A calm brand and a restless brand should not share palette mechanics.
69	- When the strategy is Committed or Drenched, color carries the brand. Don't hedge with neutrals around the edges. Commit.
70	- Don't converge across projects. If the last brand surface was restrained-on-cream, this one is not.
71	- When a cultural-symbol palette is the obvious pull, reach past it. Let the cultural reading come from typography, imagery, and copy, not the palette.
72	
73	## Layout
74	
75	- Asymmetric compositions are one option. Break the grid intentionally for emphasis.
76	- Fluid spacing with `clamp()` that breathes on larger viewports. Vary for rhythm: generous separations, tight groupings.
77	- Alternative: a strict, visible grid as the voice (brutalist / Swiss / tech-spec aesthetics). Either asymmetric or rigorously-gridded can be "designed"; the failure mode is splitting the difference into a generic centered stack.
78	- Don't default to centering everything. Left-aligned with asymmetric layouts feels more designed; a strict grid reads as confident structure. A centered-stack hero with icon-title-subtitle cards reads as template.
79	- When cards ARE the right affordance, use `grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(280px, 1fr))` for breakpoint-free responsiveness.
80	
81	## Imagery
82	
83	Brand surfaces lean on imagery. A restaurant, hotel, magazine, or product landing page without any imagery reads as incomplete, not as restrained. A solid-color rectangle where a hero image should go is worse than a representative stock photo.
84	
85	**When the brief implies imagery (restaurants, hotels, magazines, photography, hobbyist communities, food, travel, fashion, product), you must ship imagery.** Zero images is a bug, not a design choice. "Restraint" is not an excuse. If the approved comp or brief is image-led, ship real project assets, generated raster assets, or a credible canvas/SVG/WebGL scene. Do not replace photographic, architectural, product, or place imagery with generic CSS panels, decorative diagrams, cards, bullets, or copy.
86	
87	- **For greenfield work without local assets, use stock imagery.** Unsplash is the default. The URL shape is `https://images.unsplash.com/photo-{id}?auto=format&fit=crop&w=1600&q=80`. **Verify the URLs before referencing them.** If you have an image-search MCP, web-fetch tool, or browser access, use it to find real photo IDs and confirm they resolve. Guessed IDs (even ones that look real) often 404 and ship as broken-image placeholders. Without a verification path, pick fewer photos you're confident exist over more that you guessed; never substitute colored `<div>` placeholders.
88	- **Search for the brand's physical object**, not the generic category: "handmade pasta on a scratched wooden table" beats "Italian food"; "cypress trees above a limestone hotel facade at dusk" beats "luxury hotel".
89	- **One decisive photo beats five mediocre ones.** Hero imagery should commit to a mood; padding with more stock doesn't rescue an indecisive one.
90	- **Alt text is part of the voice.** "Coastal fettuccine, hand-cut, served on the terrace" beats "pasta dish".
91	
92	"Imagery" here is broader than stock photography: product screenshots, custom data visualizations, generated SVG, and canvas/WebGL scenes are all imagery. Text-only pages where typography alone carries the entire visual weight are the failure mode.
93	
94	## Motion
95	
96	- One well-orchestrated page-load with staggered reveals beats scattered micro-interactions, when the brand invites it. Tech-minimal brands often skip entrance motion entirely; the restraint is the voice.
97	- For collapsing/expanding sections, transition `grid-template-rows` rather than `height`.
98	
99	## Brand bans (on top of the shared absolute bans)
100	
101	- Monospace as lazy shorthand for "technical / developer." If the brand isn't technical, mono reads as costume.
102	- Large rounded-corner icons above every heading. Screams template.
103	- Single-family pages that picked the family by reflex, not voice. (A single family chosen deliberately is fine.)
104	- All-caps body copy. Reserve caps for short labels and headings.
105	- Timid palettes and average layouts. Safe = invisible.
106	- Zero imagery on a brief that implies imagery (restaurant, hotel, food, travel, fashion, photography, hobbyist). Colored blocks where a hero photo belongs.
107	- Defaulting to editorial-magazine aesthetics (display serif + italic + drop caps + broadsheet grid) on briefs that aren't magazine-shaped. Editorial is ONE aesthetic lane, not the default brand aesthetic.
108	- Repeated tiny uppercase tracked labels above every section heading. A single strong kicker can be voice; repeating it as section grammar is AI scaffolding unless it's a deliberate, named brand system.
109	
110	## Brand permissions
111	
112	Brand can afford things product can't. Take them.
113	
114	- Ambitious first-load motion. Reveals, scroll-triggered transitions, typographic choreography.
115	- Single-purpose viewports. One dominant idea per fold, long scroll, deliberate pacing.
116	- Typographic risk. Enormous display type, unexpected italic cuts, mixed cases, hand-drawn headlines, a single oversize word as a hero.
117	- Unexpected color strategies. Palette IS voice; a calm brand and a restless brand should not share palette mechanics.
118	- Art direction per section. Different sections can have different visual worlds if the narrative demands it. Consistency of voice beats consistency of treatment.
119

1	# Motion smoothness — why a page that renders correctly can still look cheap
2	
3	Anton, r7 (FEEDBACK.md F-012): *"scrolleffekten renderade som den skulle, men det såg
4	hackigt och billigt gjort ut."* The measured answer is F-013. Read this before writing
5	any scroll-driven motion, and read it again before "fixing" motion that someone has
6	called janky — because **two different faults produce that same sentence**, and the cure
7	for one does nothing for the other.
8	
9	## The two faults
10	
11	| | The value steps | The page drops frames |
12	|---|---|---|
13	| What you see | Motion advances in visible notches | Motion stutters and lags the hand |
14	| What the clock says | 60 fps, nothing wrong | frame p95 well over 20 ms |
15	| Where it comes from | A raw scroll value written 1:1 | Too much work per frame |
16	| What fixes it | Damp the value (`--sc-ps`) | Cut the work (`performance.md`) |
17	
18	Measure both before changing anything: `scripts/motion_probe.py` reports frame time and
19	value continuity in one run. Guessing which fault you have is how a session spends an
20	afternoon smoothing something that was never stepping.
21	
22	## Fault 1 — the raw value
23	
24	`scrollcraft.js` damps exactly two things: the video playhead (lerp 0.18, deadband,
25	seek coalescing) and the pointer devices `tilt` / `magnet`. Its own docstring explains
26	why: *"wheel events do not arrive at a constant rate and a 1:1 write reproduces every
27	gap in them."*
28	
29	That reasoning is right, and the engine does not apply it to `--sc-p`. Everything
30	`read()` writes — `--sc-p` itself, cue opacity, parallax, pan, kinetic units,
31	`clip-path`, drift — is written 1:1 from raw scroll position, on the scroll event
32	behind a one-frame rAF guard. On a mouse wheel the value stands still between notches
33	and then jumps.
34	
35	Two things make it worse:
36	
37	- **`--sc-p` is an unregistered custom property.** To CSS it is a string, so it never
38	  interpolates, and no `@property` registration exists anywhere in the engine.
39	- **`scrollcraft.css` sets `transition: none`** on `[data-sc-cue]` and `[data-sc-copy]`
40	  once `.sc-ready` lands. That is deliberate — JS owns the value — but it means nothing
41	  bridges the gap between two writes.
42	
43	**F-011 did not cause this.** `var reduce = false` turned the playhead lerp *on*
44	(rate 1.0 → 0.18). `reduce` gates ten sites in the engine and every one is a disable
45	branch. The stepping is architectural and predates the override.
46	
47	### The rule
48	
49	> **Bespoke motion reads `--sc-ps`, never raw `--sc-p`, whenever it drives something the
50	> eye sees move** — `transform`, `object-position`, `clip-path`, `mask-position`,
51	> `background-position`. Cue opacity may read `--sc-p`.
52	
53	`--sc-ps` is published by `scripts/scroll/sc-smooth.js`, copied in beside the engine and
54	loaded after it. The engine is never edited (`scroll/NOTE.md`: copy, never edit). The
55	shim lerps at 0.16 per frame with a 0.0005 deadband, registers `--sc-ps` as a real
56	`<number>` so CSS can interpolate it, stops its own rAF loop when nothing is moving, and
57	sets `will-change` **only while an act is actually in motion** — correcting the engine
58	CSS's seven class-level promotions, which `motion.md` § Bans forbids.
59	
60	A page's own rAF painters (`paintHeroPool`, `paintMotion`, a word scrub) read `--sc-ps`
61	too. `?preview=` modes set `window.__scFreezeMotion = true`, and the shim then tracks the
62	raw value exactly so a screenshot shows the formed state, not a lerp in flight.
63	
64	Measured, same motion, same wheel cadence (`tests/motion/`):
65	
66	| | frame p95 | staircase | largest single-frame step |
67	|---|---|---|---|
68	| `staircase.html` (raw `--sc-p` → `rotateY`) | 16.7 ms | 18 | 5.6 % |
69	| `smooth.html` (lerped) | 16.7 ms | **0** | **1.4 %** |
70	
71	The frame clock is identical in both. The difference is entirely in the value.
72	
73	## Fault 2 — the page is genuinely slow
74	
75	Damping a value on a page that cannot hold 60 fps just makes a smooth curve arrive late.
76	V3b, measured 2026-09-08 with no CPU throttling at all: frame p95 49.9 ms, 62 frames over
77	33 ms, 4.9 MB transferred, 19 font files, 17 long tasks during scroll, four elements with
78	a resting `will-change`. See `performance.md` for the budget and `scripts/perf_probe.py`
79	for the measurement.
80	
81	## Pace — the third thing people call "not smooth"
82	
83	From upstream scroll-craft's `worldflight.md` § 7c, the only place in the corpus where
84	someone diagnosed the complaint to root cause: *"Two separate faults get described as
85	'it doesn't feel smooth', and only one of them is smoothing."*
86	
87	- **Inconsistent pace is the worse one.** Across a multi-act or multi-leg sequence,
88	  `rate = weight / seconds` must hold within a few percent. On the `orrery` build it
89	  varied 36 % across ten legs and the owner's word for it was "not smooth"; evened to
90	  6 %, the same footage read as one continuous move.
91	- **Too fast reads as cheap.** For a fly-through, 0.21–0.22 vh per second of film is the
92	  floor. The per-8-seconds guardrail is a dead-scroll floor, not a taste target.
93	- **Damping and weights fix different halves.** *"The damping is what removes wheel
94	  judder; the weights are what remove the surging."* For a worldflight use
95	  `data-sc-lerp` **0.12**, not the 0.18 default, and widen `data-sc-seam` to ~0.16.
96	
97	`motion_probe.py` reports `max_step` per act, so an act that surges relative to its
98	neighbours shows up as a spread across runs rather than as a feeling. Full port, with
99	the weight arithmetic and the worldflight knob values: [`scroll/pace.md`](scroll/pace.md).
100	
101	## The bar
102	
103	A signature act is not finished until, at 4× CPU throttling:
104	
105	- `staircase = 0`
106	- `max_step ≤ 3 %` of the value's own range
107	- frame p95 ≤ 20 ms, zero frames over 33 ms
108	- both scroll directions measured, not just downward
109	
110	## What the harness still cannot tell you
111	
112	Upstream's `verify.md` says it plainly: *"Whether the motion is smooth. Contiguous frames
113	prove the clip advances; they do not prove it advances evenly."* `motion_probe.py` closes
114	most of that gap and does not close all of it. Watch the contact sheet for a move that
115	lurches, reverses, or stalls in the middle, and watch the sparkline the probe writes: a
116	curve with a flat shoulder is an act that stops dead mid-travel, which no single number
117	reports.
118	
119	One known, accepted inconsistency: `scripts/scroll/scrollcraft.css` line 98 still carries
120	`@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { html { scroll-behavior: auto } }`. It only
121	disables smooth anchor jumping and touches no act, and the engine is never edited, so it
122	stays — documented here rather than silently tolerated.
123

125

127	[`performance.md`](performance.md) ·
128	[`motion.md`](motion.md) · `scripts/motion_probe.py` · `scripts/scroll/sc-smooth.js` ·

1	# The device kit, condensed
2	
3	Nine ways scroll can drive the page. Pick per beat, never per page: ≥4 device
4	families, never the same one twice running. Every act publishes `--sc-p` (0–1)
5	on itself, so bespoke CSS can ride the same value the kit devices use. Full
6	depth, worked examples, and every trap: `upstream/scroll-craft/.../references/devices.md`.
7	
8	| # | Device | Syntax | Span / rate | One-line rule |
9	|---|---|---|---|---|
10	| 1 | `scrub` | `data-sc-act="scrub" data-sc-span="2.6" data-sc-dwell="0.35"` on the section; `data-sc-scrub data-sc-src="…"` on the `<video>` | span 2.2–3.0 for a hero | ≤2 per page. The wheel scrubs a pre-rendered clip; spend it on the open |
11	| 2 | `pin` | `data-sc-act="pin" data-sc-span="3"` | span ≥1.2 (below that, progress jumps 0→1 in one notch) | The frame holds, copy states cross over inside it |
12	| 3 | `pan` | `data-sc-act="pan" data-sc-span="3.2"`; rail gets `data-sc-pan="0.08"` | ~1vh per item + 1 | Lateral = breadth, not hierarchy. Overflow must be measured, not assumed |
13	| 4 | `reveal` | `data-sc-reveal="up|down|left|right|iris" data-sc-reveal-at="0.15 0.55"` | — | `clip-path` wipe = change of state. `iris` once per page at most |
14	| 5 | `kinetic` | `data-sc-kinetic="lines|words|chars"` on a cued heading | — | Lines almost always right, chars ~never. One kinetic headline per act |
15	| 6 | `parallax` | `data-sc-parallax="-0.6"` | rate is **hundreds of px total travel**, not a fraction — usable range 0.3–1.5 (framed), 1–2 (full-bleed) | Never on body copy. 3 layers is plenty |
16	| 7 | `count` | `data-sc-count="0 4,200" data-sc-count-at="0.1 0.5"` | 1.2–1.8s outside an act (`data-sc-count-ms`) | Only real numbers. No verified figure, no counter |
17	| 8 | `flow` + `in` | `data-sc-in data-sc-stagger="70"` on the wrap | stagger 30–80ms | The rest of the page. Fires once, opacity+14px rise, ~620ms ease-out |
18	| 9 | pointer: `tilt` / `magnet` / `spotlight` | `data-sc-tilt="7"` (5–9°), `data-sc-magnet="0.28"` (0.2–0.35, CTA only), `data-sc-spotlight` (publishes `--sc-mx`/`--sc-my`) | — | Gated to `(hover:hover) and (pointer:fine)`. Never gated on reduced motion (F-011, superseded 2026-09-07) |
19	
20	`drift` (`data-sc-drift="#0A0806"` on an act) is not a device, it's a
21	property: the page ground interpolates toward it while the act is live. 3–5
22	stops, one theme family. On a page of many *short* acts several can be
23	part-way through at once — paint grounds per section instead of drifting; see
24	upstream §10.
25	
26	## The cue contract — what verification actually catches you on
27	
28	`data-sc-cue="from [to [rampIn [rampOut]]]"`, all in act progress 0–1.
29	
30	| Form | Behaviour |
31	|---|---|
32	| `"0.2"` | fades in at 0.2, **holds to the end of the act** |
33	| `"0.1 0.6"` | in, plateau, out (ramps default 30% of window each) |
34	| `"0 0.78 0"` | **greet**: full opacity at act start, then fades — the hero form |
35	| `"0 1 0 0"` | **greet and hold**: full at p=0, no ramp either end |
36	
37	**The plateau is the point.** Without one, a cue is a triangle that touches full
38	opacity for a single instant, so the reader has to stop on exactly the right
39	pixel to see the line at full strength and every heading reads slightly faded.
40	`"0.1 0.9 0.15 0.4"` — fast in, long slow out — is the confident form. Cue
41	windows on a pinned act **overlap by design**, roughly 15% of the act: the
42	outgoing line is still fading while the next arrives, and a gap between cues
43	reads as a loading failure.
44	
45	Five rules, each one a real bug this fixture has caught:
46	
47	- **A hero cue needs the greet form.** A plain `"0 0.7"` means the first
48	  screen every visitor sees has no headline on it.
49	- **The last act's cue must hold** (one value). A two-value close cue fades
50	  the CTA out before the page ends.
51	- **Only the last act may hold.** A one-value cue on a *middle* pinned act
52	  stays lit through the whole un-pin slide — the line travels a full viewport
53	  up, crosses fixed chrome, overlaps the next section. Invisible until
54	  measured; shows up as a contrast failure nobody meant.
55	- **Ground or greet.** A pinned stage is fully visible ~1vh *before* its own
56	  progress leaves 0. A plain two-value first cue shows an empty stage for
57	  that whole travel — give the act a ground (image/colour already doing
58	  work) or open with a greet cue.
59	- **Clip time ≠ cue time.** A `scrub` clip is mapped across the stage's
60	  *entire visible life* (default), not across the pinned travel, because the
61	  stage is on screen for a viewport before the pin starts and after it ends.
62	  Cues keep using `p` (they belong to the pin); the clip uses a separately
63	  computed `vp`. Reaching for `data-sc-clip-map="travel"` reintroduces the
64	  freeze — there's almost no reason to.
65	
66	Two more that a harness will not catch by itself:
67	
68	- **Pan overflow must be measured, not assumed.** The rail travels exactly
69	  `scrollWidth - viewport`; a rail narrower than the viewport travels **zero**
70	  and the act reads as a still. `rail.scrollWidth - innerWidth` — check it,
71	  don't guess.
72	- **Parallax rate is hundreds of pixels total, not a viewport fraction** — see
73	  the table above. A rate of 0.35 across three viewport-heights of scroll is
74	  35px: invisible.
75	
76	Composing an act: devices stack (a pinned stage can hold a scrub clip, a
77	parallax layer, a kinetic headline, a spotlight at once), but one thing is the
78	reason the act exists — say that thing in one sentence or the act has none.
79	
80	## The playhead is lerped (§1)
81	
82	The mechanism the whole kit's smoothness rests on, and the one F-012 kept
83	being blamed on. **Scroll never writes `currentTime`.** It writes a *target*,
84	and a standalone rAF loop walks the clip toward that target at a fixed
85	fraction per frame:
86	
87	> *"Wheel events do not arrive at a constant rate, so a 1:1 write reproduces
88	> every gap in them and the clip reads as a stutter rather than a glide."*
89	
90	Three mechanisms, all on by default:
91	
92	- **Lerp 0.18 per frame.** `data-sc-lerp` overrides it, on the mount root for
93	  the whole page or on a single `<video>`. **Clamped to 0.02–1 and never read
94	  as 0** — a 0 lerp is a playhead that never moves. Reach for an override only
95	  when a page's clips are short enough that 0.18 visibly lags the hand.
96	  Worldflight wants 0.12 instead; see [`pace.md`](pace.md).
97	- **Deadband: 8 ms desktop, 20 ms mobile.** A write smaller than that costs a
98	  seek and shows nothing; on a phone it costs more than it shows.
99	- **Seek coalescing.** No seek is queued while the decoder is still resolving
100	  the last one. *"A fast flick otherwise piles seeks up and freezes the clip."*
101	
102	An offscreen clip that has already reached its target stops being touched at
103	all. (Upstream states the offscreen skip without a threshold value; the 0.002
104	figure belongs to `shoot.mjs`'s settle test, below, not to this skip.)
105	
106	This applies to **every** scrub clip on the page, act or worldflight. It is
107	also why the shooter waits for the playhead to arrive before each frame:
108	
109	> *"A frame captured mid-lerp is a frame the page never actually holds."*
110	
111	`shoot.mjs` settles on `|current − target| < 0.002 && !seeking`. Any harness
112	the chain runs against a scrubbed page inherits that requirement — a
113	screenshot taken mid-lerp makes the run unrepeatable, not merely imprecise.
114	
115	Upstream also drops the damping to 1.0 (no smoothing at all) under reduced
116	motion. **That branch does not port: F-011.** The lerp is unconditional here,
117	which is the correct behaviour anyway — it is a smoothing mechanism, not an
118	effect, and turning it off is what produces the stepping fault.
119	
120	## Layered scenes: where the premium feel comes from (§6)
121	
122	Ported from `devices.md` § 6, measured off a reference premium site and proven
123	on a live build. A flat page moves as one sheet; a layered page is a stack of
124	cut-out planes sliding past each other, and *"the eye reads that differential
125	motion as depth before it reads anything else."* It is the single biggest
126	difference between a page that feels built and one that feels assembled, and
127	it costs three transparent images and a multiplier each.
128	
129	- **Plan the planes back to front.** Far ridge, mid ridge, the product, then a
130	  **foreground plane in front of the product**. The product sits between mid
131	  and front, so the foreground overtakes it as the reader scrolls. That
132	  overtaking is the move.
133	- **Small rate differences, not big ones.** The reference hero lags the far
134	  plane **31%** behind the page, the mid plane **17%**, the product **20%**,
135	  and foreground and copy travel at exactly **1×**. Adjacent planes differ by
136	  **10–30%**. Larger stops reading as distance and starts reading as things
137	  sliding around. **Copy always rides at 1×.**
138	- **Shape the foreground for the product.** A straight-edged foreground covers
139	  the product's CTA within a few hundred pixels of scroll. Cut it so it dips
140	  where the product is and rises at the edges, and the button stays in view
141	  two to three times as long.
142	- **Every plane is solid below its silhouette.** Cut-out art that fades to
143	  transparent at the bottom lets the plane behind show through as the planes
144	  separate. Fill each column solid from its first opaque pixel down.
145	- **Fade the section floor.** Planes travel past the section's bottom edge and
146	  are clipped there. A gradient to the page ground over the last 200–300 px,
147	  layered above every plane, hides the clip line at any scroll position.
148	
149	Three traps, each of which cost a round of fixes:
150	
151	- A global `img { max-width: 100% }` shrinks an absolutely positioned plane to
152	  the viewport on phones, so the far layer never shows. **Planes carry
153	  `max-width: none` and a fixed pixel width.**
154	- **Never `transition: transform` on a parallaxed element.** A reveal class is
155	  the usual culprit. The transition eases every per-frame scroll write over
156	  its own duration, and on a phone that reads as the product lagging a full
157	  second behind the thumb. Parallaxed elements transition **opacity only**.
158	- Replacing a plane's art under the same filename ships nothing to a phone
159	  holding the old bytes. **New art gets a new name.**
160	
161	`data-sc-parallax` and a raw scroll multiplier are the same tool in different
162	units. What matters is the **ratio between planes**, not the absolute travel.
163	
164	## The premium fade-in, exactly (§8)
165	
166	The `flow` + `in` device is most of the page, so its defaults decide how the
167	page feels between the acts:
168	
169	| Ingredient | Value |
170	|---|---|
171	| Opacity | 0 → 1 |
172	| Rise | **~14 px** |
173	| Duration | **~620 ms**, ease-out |
174	| Stagger | **30–80 ms**, children in reading order |
175	| Trigger | IntersectionObserver, `-12%` bottom root margin, **fires once** |
176	
177	- **A fade with no rise reads as a loading glitch.** A rise **past 24 px reads
178	  as a slide.** 14 px is the band, not a starting point to tune upward.
179	- The `-12%` margin fires the reveal when the reader is looking, not when the
180	  first pixel clears the fold.
181	- `data-sc-in` is what the engine watches. Without it nothing fires and the
182	  stagger children stay hidden.
183	- **Content that re-hides on the way back up is a defect, not an effect.**
184	- *"Larger, slower, or bouncier is never more premium; the restraint is the
185	  signal."*
186	
187	**A flow section directly after a pinned act takes reduced padding.** The
188	pinned stage needs a full viewport to scroll off, and full `--sc-section`
189	padding on top of that delays the flow section's first content by another
190	screen. The harness will not call it dead scroll — correctly, the stage is
191	moving — and the reader still sees a near-empty screen. Cut the block padding
192	there and start the first reveal near `p = 0`.
193	
194	## Rail settle on `pan` (§3)
195	
196	Lateral travel alone reads as a slideshow on rails. **Give the rail's items a
197	staggered settle driven from `--sc-p`** and they read as a drawer being
198	pulled instead.
199	
200	- **Exempt the first item** — a `pan` act needs its opening content already
201	  present.
202	- **Floor the opacity around 0.55**, so a not-yet-settled card reads as
203	  arriving rather than as failing to load.
204	
205	Upstream gates the settle to `prefers-reduced-motion` — **utgår, F-011**.
206	The settle always runs. What *does* survive from
207	the same passage is the reachability requirement, which is not a motion
208	preference at all: a `pan` rail's transform **is** the navigation, so nothing
209	may zero it and park the act on its first screenful. Every item in a rail
210	stays reachable, and that is checked on the sheet, not assumed.
211	
212	Two more, from the same section:
213	
214	- **Card copy is read while cropped.** Items enter and leave through the
215	  viewport edges, so a heading is half-shown for most of its life, and two
216	  half-headings side by side can read as a third word (`TRACE` beside
217	  `EVALUATE` becoming `RE EVALUATE`). Keep card headings to one or two short
218	  words and expect every line to be read partially cut off.
219	- If three items do not reach half a viewport of overflow, **the fix is more
220	  rail, not wider cards**: put the act's heading in as the first item and a
221	  closing note as the last. Both earn their place, and they add the width the
222	  travel needs.
223	
224	## Devices that cannot share an element (§9)
225	
226	**`magnet`, `parallax` and `cue` all write `transform`.** The magnet writes
227	every frame in its own rAF loop, so it silently wins and the cue's entrance
228	rise is discarded — a visible animation lost to a race, with nothing in the
229	console.
230	
231	- On a magnetic CTA, set **`data-sc-rise="0"`** so the cue writes a no-op
232	  instead of losing to the magnet.
233	- A cued element that wants its own continuous transform drives an **inner
234	  wrapper** from `--sc-p` in CSS, rather than stacking a second device on the
235	  same node.
236	
237	All three pointer devices **interpolate toward** the pointer rather than
238	tracking it directly: *"direct tracking reads as artificial because it carries
239	no momentum."* They stay gated to `(hover: hover) and (pointer: fine)` so
240	touch never fires a false hover — that gate is a pointer-capability query, not
241	a motion preference, and it stands.
242	The reduced-motion half of the same sentence does not port (F-011).
243	
244	## Kinetic type: the mask and the re-split (§5)
245	
246	Each unit slides up from **behind a mask**, so it enters from a clean edge
247	rather than simply fading.
248	
249	- **Line masks must reserve room for descenders.** A mask clipped to the line
250	  box shears the tails off g, y, p and j, *"and that is the single most common
251	  way this effect looks broken."*
252	- **Line splitting measures real line boxes, so it re-runs after
253	  `document.fonts.ready`.** Do not call it on text still loading its face. The
254	  same `fonts.ready` handle earns its place twice over: a webfont swapping in
255	  changes the measured height of every copy block, so anything sized against
256	  those blocks (a scrim plate, a rail) is wrong until it re-measures.
257	- Lines are almost always right; words for a short punch line; characters
258	  approximately never, *"because it turns reading into waiting."*
259	- **One kinetic headline per act, at most.**
260	
261	## What makes a `count` land (§7)
262	
263	- **Ease out, hard.** A cubic ease-out, so most of the distance goes by in the
264	  first third and the last digits settle slowly. *"A linear count reads as a
265	  slot machine."*
266	- **1.2–1.8 s.** Under a second and the reader misses that it moved; past two
267	  and they are waiting for a number they have already guessed.
268	- **Fires at half visibility, once**, so the reader is looking at it when it
269	  starts, and it never re-runs on the way back up.
270	- **Pair it with the fade.** A counter inside a `data-sc-in` stack rises in
271	  with its label and starts ticking as it arrives — *"the same numbers static
272	  on the page read as a spreadsheet."*
273	- Write the target exactly as it should render, commas included; the engine
274	  strips them before parsing and applies `tabular-nums` so the layout does not
275	  jitter.
276	
277	**A concept, fictional or pre-launch brand has no verified figures, so it has
278	no counters.** The device suits a SaaS or agency page and will look good in
279	the score table, *"which is exactly the trap: every number you could put in it
280	would be invented."* Decide this before designing an act around a number, not
281	after. Real brand, real stats, or a different device.
282	
283	## Appendix: pattern vocabulary
284	
285	Named patterns from taste-skill § 10, carried here so orchestrator, builder
286	and reviewer name the same thing. It is a **vocabulary, not a menu** — several
287	entries below are banned as directions elsewhere in the chain (glassmorphism,
288	holographic foil, carousels, gooey menus) and appear here only so a critique
289	can say which trope it is refusing.
290	
291	- **Hero** — Asymmetric Split · Editorial Manifesto · Video/Media Mask ·
292	  Kinetic-Type · Curtain-Reveal · Scroll-Pinned.
293	- **Nav** — Dock Magnification · Magnetic Button (`data-sc-magnet`) · Gooey
294	  Menu · Dynamic Island · Contextual Radial · Floating Speed Dial · Mega Menu
295	  Reveal.
296	- **Layout** — Bento Grid · Masonry · Chroma Grid · Split-Screen Scroll ·
297	  Sticky-Stack Sections.
298	- **Cards** — Parallax Tilt Card (`data-sc-tilt`) · Spotlight Border Card
299	  (`data-sc-spotlight`) · Glassmorphism Panel · Holographic Foil ·
300	  Tinder Swipe Stack · Morphing Modal.
301	- **Scroll** — Sticky Scroll Stack · Horizontal Scroll Hijack (= `pan`) ·
302	  Locomotive / Sequence Scroll (= `scrub`) · Zoom Parallax · Scroll Progress
303	  Path · Liquid Swipe Transition.
304	- **Galleries** — Dome Gallery · Coverflow Carousel · Drag-to-Pan Grid ·
305	  Accordion Image Slider · Hover Image Trail · Glitch Effect Image.
306	- **Type** — Kinetic Marquee · **Text Mask Reveal** (massive type as a
307	  transparent window onto video — this is K2's letter-window) · Text Scramble
308	  · Circular Text Path · Gradient Stroke Animation · Kinetic Typography Grid.
309	- **Micro** — Particle Explosion Button · Liquid Pull-to-Refresh · Skeleton
310	  Shimmer · Directional Hover-Aware Button · Ripple Click · Animated SVG Line
311	  Drawing · Mesh Gradient Background · Lens Blur Depth.

313	Names alone are not permission. A pattern still has to clear the fingerprint
314	gate, the register, and `../motion.md` before it ships.
315	
316	## Never restyle the engine's classes (AB06, 2026-09-03)
317	
318	Theme the engine only through its six colour tokens and two fonts. A project rule on
319	`.sc-stage`, `.sc-copy`, `.sc-scrim` or any other `.sc-*` class silently wins over the
320	engine: the console then says `[scrollcraft] act "…" will not pin: its stage computes
321	position:relative` and every pinned act scrolls away, leaving its spacer as dead scroll.
322	Read the console for `[scrollcraft]` warnings before anything else in Step 5, and run
323	`scripts/scroll_verify.py` — a blind one-shot cannot see either. The engine is opt-in per
324	grammar (scrub, pin, pan); a page that keeps the chain's own single set-piece + shared

1	# The eight page grammars
2	
3	Condensed from `upstream/scroll-craft/.../references/uniqueness.md` §2 — read
4	that file for the full text, the worked "four sites, one template" finding,
5	and the reasoning behind each forbid. A grammar is the page's organising
6	logic, not its palette: two pages in the same grammar feel related no matter
7	how far apart their worlds are. Pick exactly one; never blend two.
8	
9	| Grammar | Fits | Scroll feels like | Forbids | Nav / hero / close | Leans on | Bans |
10	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
11	| **Filmic one-shot** | Single linear emotional arc — launches, consumer products | A film pushing through, no seams | Visible sequence, hard cuts, more than one entry point | Fixed minimal bar; full-bleed scrub hero, corner headline; pinned spotlight close, magnetic CTA | `scrub`, `pin`, `drift`, `kinetic` | Nothing structural — carries a burden of proof instead |
12	| **Chaptered editorial** | Long-form substance — method, manifesto, founder story | Turning pages, hard cuts between chapters | Continuous `drift`, full-bleed scrub hero, magnetic CTA, centred hero copy | No fixed bar; folio in margin; title-page hero (no media); colophon close, CTA as running text | `flow`+`in`, `reveal` at boundaries, `parallax` in a column, `count` in prose | `scrub` beyond one chapter, `spotlight`, `magnet` |
13	| **Live surface** | Software, tools, dashboards — the demo IS the argument | Operating something, panels populate | Any marketing chrome, full-bleed photography, kinetic headlines | App chrome (sidebar/tabs) as nav; hero is the product mid-state; close is a real input field | `pin`, `count` on real telemetry, pointer devices in-product | `scrub`, `kinetic`, `spotlight`, `drift` past two stops |
14	| **Continuous world** | A journey with real geography — supply chain, a place, a build | Moving through one space that never cuts | Section boundaries, any act device, second stage, interpolated `drift` | Nav is a map/waypoint list; hero is an establishing position; close is arrival at a place | worldflight legs, `data-sc-linger`, `sc:waypoint` | Every act device, `flow`, `pan`, hard cuts, `src` swaps |
15	| **Typographic poster** | A brand whose asset is a sentence — manifestos, agencies | Words at wildly different weights, rhythm from scale | Photographic ground, scrims, cards, decorative motion | Wordmark at composition scale; hero is one word/line at extreme scale; close inverts to smallest type, plain link | `kinetic`, `pin` with `--sc-p`-driven scale, `reveal` as a wipe | `scrub`, `pan` rails, `tilt`, `parallax` on text |
16	| **Gallery / catalog** | A range — products, portfolio, menu, materials | Walking a room, objects at their own pace | Argument-shaped pinned type, single hero claim, persuasion copy | Nav is an index that jumps; hero is object one, already labelled; close is last object or inquiry-as-label | `pan` as the spine, `reveal` per object, `tilt`, `count` | `kinetic` headlines, `spotlight`, `magnet`, >1 `scrub` |
17	| **Split stage** | Any two-sided argument — before/after, manual vs automated | Watching a balance tip toward a resolve | Full-bleed before the resolve, centred copy, symmetric close | No bar; divider IS the chrome; hero shows the split 50/50; close is the collapse to one column | `pin` with divider from `--sc-p`, `reveal` per side, real `count` | `pan`, `spotlight`, `magnet`, >1 `scrub`, `drift` |
18	| **Rhythmic cutlist** | Energy brands — streetwear, sport, events, music | A cut every second, 12–20 short sections | Any act >~1.4vh, `dwell`>0.1, `pin`, overlapping cues | Loud/marquee bar; hero cuts to next in under a viewport; close is abrupt full bleed | `flow`+`in` at short stagger, `reveal` on nearly every section, hard `drift` steps | `pin`, `spotlight`, `magnet`, `dwell`, `parallax` |
19	
20	Cutlist's peak problem — it bans the devices a peak normally wants — is
21	solved by moving the peak into the fixed chrome layer rather than breaking
22	the grammar; see uniqueness.md §2.8.
23	
24	## Two grammars carry a hard precondition
25	
26	Both are the kind of thing that is discovered a full build too late. Check
27	them at grammar selection, not at verification.
28	
29	### Live surface: the honesty rule (§2.3)
30	
31	The page behaves like the product — *"not a screenshot of it, and not a
32	div-built fake: the actual surface, running, with scroll driving its state."*
33	`taste.md`'s ban on fake dashboards and fake terminals is **not suspended
34	here**, and this grammar is where it is most tempting to suspend it.
35	
36	> The surface has to be **real markup running real logic on real or
37	> clearly-labelled sample data.**
38	
39	That labelled-sample escape is the whole way in for a **concept product**:
40	every panel is operable markup computing its state from data arrays in the
41	page, and **the page says on its face that the scenario is a demo**. Both
42	halves are required — operable, and labelled.
43	
44	What stays banned is *"the painting of a surface"*: an image, or dummy divs,
45	posing as something that runs. **If the panels cannot actually compute, the
46	grammar is unavailable. Pick another.** This is a build-feasibility question
47	disguised as a style choice, so answer it before the score table exists.
48	
49	Note the shape of the close this implies: *"a magnetic button is the wrong
50	ending for a page that spent its whole length being a tool"* — the close is an
51	**actual input** the visitor can put a cursor in.
52	
53	### Continuous world requires worldflight (§2.4)
54	
55	> **This grammar REQUIRES worldflight mode.** `data-sc-mode="worldflight"`,
56	> one fixed stage, one spacer, legs that crossfade.
57	
58	Building it out of pinned acts is **not a lesser version of this grammar, it
59	is a different and worse page**, and it has already been tried. The owner's
60	verdict on the act-based attempt:
61	
62	> *"awful… you're literally going from scrolling down to static page and then
63	> you start scrolling down again… weird clear page lines scrolling up… very
64	> cheap looking."*
65	
66	Every one of those is the same defect. **A pinned act is a block in the
67	document; a document made of blocks has seams; and a world with seams is not a
68	world.** Do not reach for `scrub` acts here, however long the spans are made.
69	
70	This is also the expensive one: *"a single unbroken flight is the most fragile
71	thing you can build"*, the seam law is not optional, and the build should be
72	budgeted with a reroll in it. Choose this grammar only when the brief is
73	literally about travel through a place. Its pace bar has its own file —
74	[`pace.md`](pace.md).
75	
76	## Register × grammar fit
77	
78	The six registers are `../../SKILL.md` § The craft floor's own list. Each row
79	below is 2–3 grammars that genuinely fit that register, plus one grammar that
80	reads as a mismatch and the one-line reason why.
81	
82	| Register | Fits | Mismatch (and why) |
83	|---|---|---|
84	| **Editorial print** | Chaptered editorial (the register's native shape); Gallery/catalog (museum-label copy is already this register's voice); Typographic poster (a manifesto-led atelier) | Rhythmic cutlist — a loud marquee bar and hard-cut energy contradicts the register's restraint and apparatus |
85	| **Cinematic dark** | Filmic one-shot (linear narrative arc, hospitality/launch); Continuous world (atmosphere as geography — a restaurant, a hotel); Gallery/catalog (a menu as a walkable collection) | Typographic poster — the grammar bans photographic ground outright, and cinematic dark's whole effect is atmosphere built from photography |
86	| **Illustrated dark** | Typographic poster (strong verbal identity paired with drawn forms); Gallery/catalog (a set of speaker/object portraits as objects); Chaptered editorial (a programme read as chapters) | Live surface — the grammar bans marketing chrome and kinetic headlines, which is exactly the illustrated-identity apparatus this register is built from |
87	| **Modern clean** | Live surface (the subject is precision — an instrument, a technical firm); Split stage (a before/after comparison, cost vs saving); Typographic poster (minimal photography, the claim carries it) | Rhythmic cutlist — a loud, marqueed, cut-every-second page fights a register whose whole case is calm precision |
88	| **Warm photographic** | Filmic one-shot (a consumer/hospitality arc); Continuous world (a journey through a place — harbour, guesthouse); Gallery/catalog (rooms or dishes as a walkable range) | Typographic poster — same conflict as cinematic dark: the register's asset is the photograph, and the grammar has no photographic ground at all |
89	| **Historical art** | Gallery/catalog (museum labels are this grammar's literal copy schema); Chaptered editorial (an institution that plausibly publishes an edition or catalogue); Continuous world (a journey through a collection or a period) | Rhythmic cutlist — a loud, marqueed, energy-brand grammar reads as flippant against institutional gravitas |
90	
91	Cite `upstream/scroll-craft/plugins/nateherk-design/skills/scroll-craft/references/uniqueness.md`
92	for the full grammar text, the fingerprint gate, and the signature-move rules
93	(the latter two are condensed separately in
94	[`feel-and-fingerprint.md`](feel-and-fingerprint.md)).

1	# Generated material — Higgsfield first, measured, and never on the page's behalf
2	
3	The chain generates **material**, never design. A card flip, a drawing that draws itself,
4	a divider that tips: those are CSS and scroll code, and no model produces them. What a
5	model produces is the stuff motion acts on — a cinematic still, a camera move that will
6	be scrubbed, a drawn system, a texture.
7	
8	This file owns the route, the credit gate, the fallback ladder, who may generate, and
9	what has to be true before anything is vendored.
10	
11	One correction it carries: `assets.md` § Generated illustration used to say *"No
12	animation. None of these models output multi-frame."* That is no longer true for this
13	vault. Kling 3.0, Seedance and Minimax are one MCP call away.
14	
15	## 1 · Where it sits in Step 5b
16	
17	Sources, in preference order:
18	
19	1. The product's own surface, screenshotted.
20	2. Real photography — the contact-sheet pipeline.
21	3. **Generated material**, when no sourced image can carry the picture the register needs
22	   *and* the brief names what is to be generated.
23	4. A bespoke drawn identity system.
24	5. Curated component sources, for tech surfaces.
25	
26	Generation is third, not first. A sourced photograph that holds beats a generated one,
27	and in a drawn register (zero photography, an identity built from line) a drawn system
28	beats both. "We could generate it" is not a reason; "nothing sourced can be this" is.
29	
30	## 2 · Route
31	
32	Run `models_explore` (`action: "recommend"`, with the goal and the input kind) before the
33	first call of every run. The catalogue moves, and the CLI and MCP front ends do not even
34	use the same model ids. The table below is the starting point, measured in r7.
35	
36	Measured against the live catalogue 2026-09-08, with `get_cost` preflights (no jobs
37	queued). **The catalogue had already moved since r7**, which is the whole reason the
38	`models_explore` call is mandatory rather than advisory: `kling3_0` is now
39	`kling3_0_turbo` and takes a **start frame only** — the model r7 used for a locked-both-
40	ends clip no longer offers that role.
41	
42	| Need | Model | Cost | Notes |
43	|---|---|---|---|
44	| Hero/plate still, 2K, image-to-image off a real photo | `nano_banana_pro` | **2 cr** | `image_references` role; 1k/2k/4k; 21:9 available |
45	| Same, cheaper, still photoreal | `nano_banana_2` / `nano_banana` | — | Both carry `supports_unlim` |
46	| Cinematic still, up to 4K | `cinematic_studio_2_5` | — | `image` role, not `image_references` |
47	| **Scrub clip, start AND end frame locked** | **`minimax_h3_max`** | **25 cr / 10 s** | Roles `start_image` + `end_image`; 5–15 s; 480p/768p; 21:9 |
48	| Same, longer or with audio | `flux_3_video` | — | 5–20 s, 1080p, start+end, audio (turn it off) |
49	| Clip from a start frame only | `kling3_0_turbo` | — | No `end_image` role — do not use where the end state matters |
50	| Drawn / vector system, wordmarks, line figures | Recraft V4.1 | — | The only model with production-grade SVG out |
51	| Seamless texture (drafting paper, grain, weave) | `gpt_image_2` via the tiling procedure | — | Verified by a seam ratio near 1.0 |
52	| Copy motion from a driving video | `hf_mult_motion_control` | — | Genjutsu; not the legacy `motion_control` |
53	| Replace an object in a video | `hf_mult_replace_object` | — | Genjutsu |
54	
55	A 10-second locked-both-ends clip therefore costs **25 credits**, not the 17.5 r7 paid.
56	Budget from the preflight, never from this table.
57	
58	### Shape rules for a clip that will be scrubbed
59	
60	- **One continuous move, one direction, slower than feels right.** No cuts. The subject
61	  never leaves frame; nothing enters or exits.
62	- **Start state ≠ end state.** The first frame is the establishing shot, the last is the
63	  closing state. If they are the same picture the scrub has no payoff.
64	- **Pass the start image in the model's generic image-reference role, not a start-frame
65	  role**, or the clip opens frozen. r7 hit the same failure class at the other end: the
66	  last three seconds stood still.
67	- In a multi-leg clip, the next leg's start frame is the **actual decoded last frame** of
68	  the previous leg, extracted with a reverse filter — never a separately imagined
69	  "destination" still. Position continuity comes from the exact-frame handoff; velocity
70	  continuity comes from matching direction and speed on both sides.
71	- Dark, low-detail regions where copy will sit. Keep the subject away from the far edges,
72	  because a full-viewport clip is shown with `cover`.
73	- Cut phone clips portrait. A landscape clip in a portrait viewport decodes the whole
74	  frame and throws three quarters away — soft and stuttering on the phone, smooth on the
75	  desktop.
76	- Encode with a dense GOP before vendoring — see [`assets.md`](assets.md) § Encoding. A
77	  normal web encode plays perfectly and scrubs like mud.
78	- `count: 2–4` is for genuine variants of the *same* prompt and inputs. Every separate
79	  concept, emotion or camera take gets its own call.
80	
81	## 3 · The credit gate
82	
83	1. **A ceiling is written in `BRIEF.md` before anything is queued** (`generation budget: N
84	   credits`). r7 ran to 35, and Anton raised it to 36.5 with an explicit "Ja, kör pro".
85	2. **Read `balance` first.** If the balance is under twice the ceiling, report and ask
86	   before the first job.
87	3. **`get_cost: true` on every job before running it.** No generation without the cost
88	   having been read. This is why r7's log reconciles.
89	4. **Omit `use_unlim`** so the server may return `unlim_choice`; if a free allowance
90	   covers the model, put the question to Anton before spending credits. Never set
91	   `use_unlim: true` on your own initiative.
92	5. **Log every call** in `runs/<cell>/higgsfield/LOG.md`: step, model, inputs with media
93	   ids, cost, and your own reading of the frames. The log is the evidence, not memory.
94	6. **The ceiling is never passed quietly.** Reaching it means stopping, saying what
95	   remains and what it would cost, and continuing down the fallback ladder meanwhile.
96	
97	## 4 · Fallback ladder
98	
99	1. **Higgsfield** — first choice for everything generated.
100	2. **If credits are short: ChatGPT / Codex image generation**, per
101	   `impeccable/reference/codex.md` (`image_gen`, four stop points, palette before mocks).
102	   Codex produces **no video**; for moving material there is no ChatGPT fallback.
103	3. **Only then, no generation**: real photography, a drawn SVG system, or CSS art — and
104	   if the act needed a clip, the *device* changes rather than the quality. A `reveal` or
105	   `pin` built on real stills replaces a `scrub`. Shipping an empty plate because the clip
106	   would not generate is not an outcome.
107	
108	The ladder is entered only for missing credits or an unavailable service — never because
109	it is faster, and never silently: the substitution gets a row in the decision ledger with
110	its reason.
111	
112	## 5 · Who may generate
113	
114	**The orchestrator, never the builder.** Builders run headless and inherit the account
115	connector, so the restriction is mechanical: `run.py` puts a `--disallowed-tools` pattern
116	for the Higgsfield tools on the builder argv, and the builder prompt says the material is
117	already vendored under `runs/<cell>/assets/` with `credits.json`. A builder that tries
118	anyway shows up in the ledger as a denied tool call.
119	
120	The architect specifies material as an **asset lock**, never as a prompt:
121	
122	```
123	Asset role:    hero plate / texture / illustration / cutout
124	Slot:          dimensions, aspect ratio, where on the page
125	Art direction: subject, palette from the lock, light, rendering, crop
126	Avoid:         wrong palette, text in image, people, symmetric composition,
127	               mesh gradient, stock-lighting
128	```
129	
130	The lock's `Art direction` becomes the prompt and `Avoid` becomes its constraints. A
131	generated object with no asset lock does not get queued.
132	
133	## 6 · Before anything is vendored
134	
135	r7's first clip carried a hallucinated banner with unreadable characters at t=4–6 and
136	froze for its last three seconds. Neither is visible without looking at the frames.
137	
138	1. **Contact sheet** of ten evenly spaced frames, and read every one as an image. Check
139	   for: hallucinated text or signage, hands and faces (never on an Alunix page), objects
140	   entering or leaving, motion that stops, a camera that changes direction.
141	2. **Track the subject** when the act depends on something staying in frame: plot its
142	   position across the frames and confirm it moves monotonically.
143	3. **Never ship a mock crop as an asset**, and never raw output: post-process per
144	   `assets.md` — grain, an asymmetric crop, a grade.
145	4. **Provenance**: a row per generated object in `credits.json` (model, prompt, media/job
146	   id, cost, date), a `generated: <model> · post-processed` stamp in the section comment,
147	   and a visible credit line where the page itself refers to the material.
148	5. **Encode** before the file enters `assets/`.
149	
150	## 7 · Measured like every other call
151	
152	`hooks/design-vision-track.py` logs Higgsfield MCP calls as `kind: generation`;
153	`design-gate.py` denies a `generate_*` without a budget line and a preceding `get_cost`;
154	`design-stop.py` reports jobs, summed cost and models, and reconciles against
155	`credits.json`. A generation that does not appear in the ledger is a defect, not a
156	convenience.
157	
158	## 8 · Never
159	
160	- **`sync_agents`.** It uploads Anton's own skills and a synthesised personality file to
161	  Higgsfield's marketplace. It installs nothing. It is not a chain step; if Anton wants
162	  it, it is his command.
163	- **`website-builder-flow`** and the game flow. They build React 19 + TanStack Start on
164	  Cloudflare Workers and instruct the agent to stop consulting other design guidance. The
165	  chain ships single-file HTML and does not deploy.
166	- Faces or people on an Alunix page.
167	- Generated UI, generated screenshots of a product, generated logos of "customers" — the
168	  same rule as gate 46 and gate 47, with a generator attached.
169	- A generated image shipped raw.
170	- Marketplace-style claim panels (`pain_points`, `efficacy`, `endorsement`). They are
171	  fabricated marketing with a rendering step in front.
172	
173	## Related
174	
175	[`upstream/higgsfield/scroll-scrub.md`](upstream/higgsfield/scroll-scrub.md) (the scrub production spec: start/end states, seam handoff, byte budgets, blob-seek playback) · [`upstream/higgsfield/scroll-scrub-asset-video.md`](upstream/higgsfield/scroll-scrub-asset-video.md) (the ffmpeg recipes) · [`upstream/higgsfield/game-textures.md`](upstream/higgsfield/game-textures.md) (seamless tiling, verified by seam ratio) ·
